runs.title: MSC Poesia detained in Miami: why and what passengers get
runs.prompt: The cruise ship MSC Poesia was detained by the US Coast Guard at PortMiami in early November 2026, and its sailing was cancelled. Find out: (1) the specific reason the Coast Guard detained the ship, (2) when the sailing was scheduled and how many passengers were affected, and (3) what MSC Cruises has said passengers will get (refund/compensation) and who to contact. Report from public pages — the Coast Guard's own press release and the cruise line's official statement are the most authoritative. Start at the Coast Guard newsroom and the main cruise-news sites.
runs.answer: The Coast Guard detained MSC Poesia at PortMiami on Nov. 1, 2026 after a Port State Control inspection turned up "deficiencies" in onboard systems; the USCG confirmed the detention in a Nov. 3 statement but deliberately withheld the specifics, and MSC Cruises would only describe it as a "regulatory matter" it could not resolve in time. The cancelled voyage was the 11-night Caribbean/Central America sailing that was to depart Miami on Nov. 1 and return Nov. 12, 2026 — passengers had already boarded and were kept aboard more than two days before MSC cancelled on Nov. 4 (the ship's next scheduled departure, a 10-night Eastern Caribbean cruise, was Nov. 12). MSC is giving affected guests a full refund plus a 100% future cruise credit and is helping them get home; the line says guests will be contacted directly with instructions and should deal with MSC Cruises or their travel agent. I could not confirm the exact number of passengers affected — no source I could actually read published a figure (Cruise Critic and the USCG newsroom were bot-walled; the USCG release only loaded through a text proxy, and my read of it was cut off before the body).

runs.title: Kraków shooting: what happened and official updates
runs.prompt: On 7 November 2026 there was a shooting in Kraków's Main Market Square in Poland. Find out the confirmed facts, respectfully: how many people were killed and injured, what is known about the gunman and whether he was caught or shot, and where the Polish authorities are posting official updates. runs.answer: At around 15:00 on 7 November 2026 a gunman opened fire from a black, unplated Subaru that drove into Kraków's Main Market Square from Sławkowska Street, then circled the square and fled toward Kazimierz. Małopolska Police confirmed six people dead (Wikipedia's sourced account: four women and two men) and 15 injured, including two police officers; a tram on line 1 was also hit, shattering the driver's cabin window with no reported injuries there. The suspect is a 24-year-old Polish citizen in military-style tactical gear using an AR-15-style rifle; he was shot and wounded by officers in an exchange of fire (two police injured), then detained after a police chase in the Kazimierz area — prosecutors say the motive is unknown and they are checking whether he acted with others. Official updates are coming from Małopolska Police (malopolska.policja.gov.pl) and the Kraków District Prosecutor's Office via spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk, relayed live by TVN24; the national police (policja.pl) and Interior Ministry (gov.pl/web/mswia) front pages had not yet posted items when I checked, and RCB only carries alert-type notices.

runs.title: Pick the best Ocarina of Time review source
runs.prompt: Nintendo has released a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026), reportedly for the Switch 2, and reviews are coming out. I want to read a full, detailed review that is genuinely accessible without a paywall or a login. From these three candidate sources, decide which one actually lets a plain web reader see the full review text, and summarize what it says: Eurogamer, Game Informer, and The Guardian.
runs.answer: The Guardian is the source a plain reader can actually read end-to-end: its Switch 2 Ocarina of Time review (4 Nov 2026) loaded as full article text with no paywall, login or subscription prompt. The review argues the remake keeps 1998's structure and beats intact — Link still starts in Kokiri Forest, still rides Epona over the Lon Lon Ranch fence, and the intro still plays unskippably — while rebuilding the presentation with the same soft, painterly, light-dappled art style as the recent Link's Awakening-style remakes and adding fully voiced cutscenes, which purists may resist but which the reviewer finds genuinely moving. It notes the world is still split into chunks, so Hyrule Field shows lower resolution and visible pop-in, and that dungeons gain small shortcuts and quality-of-life touches rather than wholesale redesign; the verdict is that Ocarina of Time still earns its "Citizen Kane of video games" reputation and did not need reinventing. By contrast, Game Informer's page never served me its review body past the site chrome and cookie banner, and Eurogamer's page only rendered its opening section before my text extraction cut off, so I could not verify either as a complete,
